title: What If the Thames Froze Solid? It Did, and an Elephant Walked Across

scenes.text: What if the Thames froze solid? It did, and Londoners held fairs on it. An elephant walked across.
Between 1600 and 1814, the river at London froze over more than twenty times, during the Little Ice Age.
Old London Bridge helped. Its nineteen narrow arches slowed the water until it stood almost still, and froze.
1684: ice eleven inches thick for two months. Tents, a whole ox roasting, printing presses. The king bought a souvenir.
February 1814: the last fair. Nearly a dozen presses on the ice, and an elephant led across below Blackfriars Bridge.
Then the old bridge came down, the river ran faster, and the climate warmed. The Thames hasn't frozen since.

description:
What if the Thames froze solid? During the Little Ice Age it did, more than twenty times between 1400 and 1831, and Londoners held frost fairs on the ice.
Old London Bridge's nineteen narrow arches slowed the river so much it could freeze. In the Great Frost of 1683-84 the ice was up to 11 inches thick for about two months, with tents, a roast ox and printing presses selling souvenir cards; King Charles II bought one. The last fair ran from 31 January to 5 February 1814, when an elephant was led across below Blackfriars Bridge. The old bridge was demolished in 1831-32, embankments narrowed and sped up the river, and the climate warmed.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: When the 1814 ice broke up, several people drowned, and the ice floes nearly took the old bridge with them. Which river would you want to walk across? Drop your own what-if below.
